title: From Weights to Uncertainty: Shannon Entropy in Bits
concept_summary: Nonnegative weights are converted into a probability distribution by dividing each weight by the total weight. Shannon entropy H = -sum(p_i log2 p_i) measures the average uncertainty of that distribution in bits, with the convention that a zero-probability outcome contributes zero.
why_it_matters: Entropy quantifies how many bits are needed on average to describe the outcome of a random source. It is the foundation of data compression and channel capacity: a source with entropy H bits per symbol cannot be compressed below H bits per symbol on average, and a uniform distribution over n outcomes has the maximum entropy log2(n).

explanation_steps.heading: Normalize weights into probabilities
explanation_steps.body: Start with nonnegative weights w_i. Their sum W = sum(w_i) is positive. The normalized probabilities are p_i = w_i / W. This makes the p_i nonnegative and sum(p_i) = 1, so they form a valid probability distribution.

explanation_steps.heading: Entropy as average surprise
explanation_steps.body: For each outcome with probability p_i, the information content is -log2(p_i) bits. Shannon entropy is the probability-weighted average of these information contents: H = -sum(p_i log2 p_i). A certain outcome (p_i = 1) gives H = 0; a uniform distribution over n outcomes gives H = log2(n), the maximum for that n.

explanation_steps.heading: Why the zero convention matters
explanation_steps.body: When p_i = 0, the term p_i log2(p_i) is undefined as a real number, but its limiting value is 0. Shannon's formula adopts the convention that a zero-probability outcome contributes 0 to the sum. This keeps H finite and continuous as probabilities approach zero.

terms.meaning: Nonnegative weight for outcome i. Weights need not sum to 1.
Total weight, W = sum(w_i). Must be positive for normalization.
Probability of outcome i, computed as p_i = w_i / W.
Shannon entropy in bits, H = -sum(p_i log2 p_i), with 0 log2 0 treated as 0.
Base-2 logarithm, so entropy is measured in bits.

equations.explanation: Normalize nonnegative weights by their total to obtain a probability distribution.
Shannon entropy of the distribution p, measured in bits.
Convention that a zero-probability outcome contributes zero to the entropy sum.

controls.label: Weights
controls.meaning: Nonnegative weights for three outcomes. They are normalized to probabilities by dividing by their sum.

controls.label: Common scale factor
controls.meaning: Multiplies all weights by the same positive factor. Normalization removes this factor, so probabilities and entropy are unchanged.

explorations.change: Set the weights to [1, 1, 1] and then to [1, 0, 0].
explorations.observe: For [1, 1, 1], probabilities are [1/3, 1/3, 1/3] and H = log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits. For [1, 0, 0], probabilities are [1, 0, 0] and H = 0 bits.
explorations.why: This shows the two extremes: maximum uncertainty for a uniform distribution over three outcomes, and zero uncertainty when the outcome is certain.

explorations.change: Keep the weights at [1, 1, 1] and vary the common scale factor from 0.1 to 10.
explorations.observe: The scaled weights change, but the probabilities remain [1/3, 1/3, 1/3] and H remains log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits.
explorations.why: Normalization divides by the total weight, so multiplying all weights by the same positive constant cancels out. Entropy depends only on the relative proportions of the weights.

limitations: The demo uses exactly three outcomes to keep the visualization and calculations compact; the same formula applies to any finite number of outcomes.
The entropy formula assumes the probabilities are normalized to sum to 1. If the total weight is zero, normalization is undefined and entropy cannot be computed.
The convention 0 log2 0 = 0 is a limiting value, not a direct evaluation of the expression at zero.
This lesson does not derive the source coding theorem or channel capacity; it only illustrates the entropy formula and its basic properties.

source_claims.claim: Shannon entropy is H = -sum(p_i log2 p_i), where p_i are probabilities.
Entropy vanishes when the outcome is certain.
source_claims.quote: Thus only when we are certain of the outcome does H vanish.

source_claims.claim: A zero-probability outcome contributes zero to the entropy sum.

teaching_simplifications: The common scale factor control is added to demonstrate that normalization removes a common positive factor; it is not part of Shannon's original presentation.

The maximum entropy computation log2(length(probabilities)) is a standard consequence of the entropy formula for a uniform distribution, but it is not stated as a separate equation in the supplied source excerpt.
The demo uses three outcomes and a bars visualization to keep the lesson compact; Shannon's theory applies to any finite number of outcomes.

checks.name: Common scale does not change entropy
